utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom and outside. Could the witness be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Please sit down. I would like to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And Mr. Tolimir has some more questions for you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May God be on our help, and may these proceedings complete with God's will. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to wish good afternoon to the witness, and I would appreciate it if you could answer briefly to my questions, especially if you do not know the answer to a question. You can just say you don't know and that's sufficient. Thank you. Yesterday, we were discussing aerial photographs, and we will continue with that topic today. And I would like to briefly dwell on some documents in English. Could we please see 1D59. This is a statement -- or, rather, the statement that this witness provided to the French Parliamentary Committee. Can we have it on the screens, please. I would like to quote a portion of the statement. You said: "It is certain that I will be unable to answer some questions in view of the fact that the investigation is still ongoing and, under Rule 70, some information can only be disclosed with the agreement and approval of the information provider." My question: The information that you received from the United States, the aerial photos, do they fall under Rule 70 in the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is more a question for the Prosecution. I would say yes, but then when it is turned into evidence, there might be a release and a question for the Prosecution, not for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know at all how these photos were made, what type of instrument was used to make these shots? Because it is still unclear how they were -- they came into being. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The agreement is not to discuss the platform that was used to take these pictures, but if you want to highlight on the methodology used to access them, what I can tell you is that all of these pictures were provided based on a very precise request. We were framing an area where we had difficulties to find locations, and giving 10-digit grid references or a more larger area, we could ultimately have access to a photograph that would either be of immediate use for investigation, but most of the time it was to enable us to go on remote locations and find places that without the assistance of these photographs, we would have had a lot of difficulties to find.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You said just a moment ago, and you said the same thing yesterday, We received from the United States what we requested. Does that mean that they did not offer any photos to you; they just provided what you asked them to provide you with? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except one instance, this is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey said, as recorded on pages 19 and 20 of yesterday's transcript, that the United States, whenever a request was submitted, are open to provide this type of documents, and this came about when I actually objected to Mr. McCloskey's question. Thank you. In your statement before the French Parliamentarian Committee, on page 10, document 1D59, you say, and I quote: "The situation is different when secondary mass graves are concerned. One of those mass graves was discovered by Americans, who then advised us as to where that mass grave was." And then you go on to say: "We received all this information from US intelligence services." My question is this: Can you tell us, bearing in mind what Mr. McCloskey said also, what intelligence service you got this information from, in view of the fact that the US intelligence community consists of 16 different agencies? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, could you please wait until you get the floor. Now you get the floor, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I apologise. Can I clarify? Do you want me to stand and wait until I get the floor before I say, "Objection," or do I say, "Objection" first and wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think when you raise and you get up and I see you on your feet, then it's a clear indication that you want to object.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Fine, thank you. I'll endeavour to do that. I'm sorry, I've got years of bad habits otherwise, but I will -- I will correct, I promise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber will appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. This is beyond the scope of Rule 70, Mr. President, and should not be gone into. I cannot speak for the United States, but I do understand, as should Mr. Tolimir because the letters of agreement about this material have been provided to him, and going into the processes and the procedures related to them is not something the United States has agreed to allow us to discuss, even if we know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, I think you know the procedure, you know the Rules, and you should take that into account when you put questions to this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I do have that in mind, but when I said yesterday "intelligence service," there was an objection -- or, rather, a comment that it wasn't provided by the intelligence -- by an intelligence service, but, rather, by the State Department. However, here, in document 1D59, on page 10, it is explicitly said "provided by the intelligence services of the United States." In view of the fact that I intend to ask several other questions, I wanted to know which service this was obtained from and where we can get this information. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My next question is this: Mr. Ruez, was there a special liaison person who would liaise between you and the United States government and that intelligence service? Answer just yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Any discussion of specific intelligence services or intelligence service at all is absolutely off limits, as far as our agreement, the OTP's, with the United States, and whether or not that was mentioned at a French parliamentary hearing or not is not relevant, really, to this matter before us. And so I would object to this witness being required to answer any questions about intelligence services. Prior to the United States, and I hate to get them involved, frankly, but -- because I cannot speak for them and I will not, when it comes to specifics, but I do know the agreement, and I know that specific intelligence services -- intelligence services are not something that we are allowed to speak about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Coming back to the wording of your question, Mr. Tolimir, page 5, line 7 to 9, your question was: "Was there a special liaison person who would liaise between you and that intelligence service?" I think it's important to understand your question. If you are referring to a person -- if you are referring to the person -- a member of the OTP, the Prosecution, who would liaise with the state or are you referring to a person -- a representative of the United States as a liaison officer to the Prosecution, could you clarify that first, please?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour, just as you said in the latter part of what you said. I asked, Was there a special person within the OTP who was in charge of liaising with American authorities, including the American intelligence service? That was my question. And since I have the floor, I would like to point another thing out before we hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry. In the moment, you don't have the floor. You answered my question. I think it is an appropriate question if you ask for -- if there was a person in the OTP responsible for liaising with American authorities. But, please, you can't ask if this person was responsible for the contact with any intelligence service or any other organisations of the United States. If you want to ask that question related to the OTP, please then put this question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. So would you please put the question to the witness, as the Trial Chamber, and then we can hear his answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, could you help us and tell us if at the time you were employed and acted for the OTP -- I would like to wait. Now I would like to repeat the question. Can you tell the Chamber if there was at that time, when you were employed in the OTP, a special person in the OTP who was a kind of liaison officer for this contact with the American authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that answering the question would not be a violation of any Rule 70 information. It would be a disclosure of internal structure of the OTP. I don't know if this is covered by any kind of mystery or secrecy. I would feel more comfortable if someone else than me, meaning the former chief of investigations or Deputy Prosecutor at that time, would be the person answering the question. But since it's a lot of moment for a question that is quite obvious and basic, yes, for sure there was someone in charge of liaising with foreign embassies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. That was, in fact, the question. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. When I ask a question that can be answered with yes or no, I appeal to you, in view of the fact that Mr. Ruez, who used to work for the OTP and who is answering the questions, I believe he should provide the answer and not Mr. McCloskey. That's the first thing. Second, if the Rule applies to the intelligence service of the United States, then it should also apply to the intelligence service of the Republika Srpska Army, because all of the documents that we've seen here are from the intelligence service of the Republika Srpska Army. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My next question: Does the term "American National Intelligence Office" mean anything to you, which is part of the Ministry of Defence of the United States and which has its headquarters in Virginia? Now, would you -- could you answer that question? And if you don't know the answer, just say you don't know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does "KX-11" mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I apologise. I made an error. I actually meant "KH-11." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have an opportunity to read the report of the Dutch Institute for War Documents, Addendum 2? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We will not ask to have it on our screens because we've already lost a lot of time. But let me ask you this: Did you in any way check the authenticities of the photos that you received from the United States? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not assess the date, though, as I told -- when what can be seen on the pictures gives a confirmation of witness testimonies, it highlights on one aspect of what happened these days, I mean the dates the photographs are dates [sic]. And for the rest, the authenticity at least of what is on the ground, because I systematically went personally on these spots and could assess that, indeed, the photograph depicts the area we were looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. We saw yesterday the difference between --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... could you please let Judge Nyambe first put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I have a question for the witness. In answer to the question, "Did you in any way check the authenticity of the photographs that you received from the United States," your answer is, "I systematically went personally on these spots and could assess that, indeed, the photographs depict areas we were looking for." Is this the same as checking the authenticity of the pictures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a way, yes, since at least the authenticity is regarding the location the photograph is supposed to speak about. So when it is a photograph of, let's say, Nova Kasaba football pitch, for example, at least the authenticity is that the picture shows, indeed, the football pitch of Nova Kasaba and not the one of Bratunac or God knows where. So that's one aspect of the authenticity. Then the other aspect of the authenticity are the markings on it. As I said at one point, the hour can be more or less checked when you look at the shadows and when you know at what month the photograph was taken, because of the position of the sun. Then the date, for sure, is impossible to assess, but when the events that can be seen on the photograph match events that witnesses date at a certain date, it's an additional confirmation of the authenticity, as far as I see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: So your simple answer is, yes, you checked the authenticity of the pictures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let's say I naturally checked it by my activities, but the purpose was, indeed, not to believe at the first stage that it was not authentic. It's coming from a serious government source, so my assessment was, anyhow, that basically, yes, it is authentic. But then the observations on the ground and others, in my opinion, confirm that they are absolutely authentic, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, are you the proper person to be an expert able to assess authenticity?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not testify with the status of an expert, but with one of a witness, I think, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you whether you asked that authenticity be verified, so thank you. You did or you didn't?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only repeat what I previously said. There was no specific investigation launched to verify the authenticity of material provided by a state government of the US. And for the rest, what I said regarding how I could, in my opinion, confirm they were authentic, I already answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. I asked you about checking out the authenticity of the date or information. I asked you how that was done. I didn't ask you whether you did that in the field or not, so I'm satisfied with your answer. You didn't involve anybody else, so thank you, yes.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that case, I would correct. There was a large team involved in checking that, sir. It's named the Exhumation Team. Most of these pictures we used in order to find and pin-point the position of mass graves. We even were at one stage allowed to take the pictures out of the US Embassy to take them with us. This is the basic purpose to avoid walking too much in the areas where those who were delocated, the primary mass graves did put them, so in areas destroyed by war and stuffed with land-mines. So the goal was not to walk too much away from the asphalt road, as you can imagine. So the confirmation of the authenticity is coming very simply from the fact when, when you have ground dated 5th July, and when on another picture you have disturbed soil dated 25 July, when you go on that spot, you take your shovel, you dig, and you find multiple bodies, some of them with hands attached in the back, some with blindfolds, obviously non-combatants, this proves the authenticity of these pictures, as far as I am concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, all those pictures, were they in the area of responsibility of the American forces of KFOR in that part of Republika Srpska? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Negative. Half of them were in the area of responsibility of Multi-Division North, so indeed Americans, and all the area north, starting at the execution site of the dam, was under the responsibility of the Russian forces, who provided us security when we were going and finding places in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. Could you tell me whether the Russian forces belonged to Sector North of the American Division of KFOR?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ruez, did you pay for these photographs, so that the Defence can know about that? And if you did, how much?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not one dollar, as far as I am concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ask for the photographs of Muslim forces in Srebrenica from the moment the column set out to the breakthrough of the column in Baljkovici? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is how we got the one that shows fresh traces of shelling in the area of Konjevici [phoen]. It was the only one of very weak interest that we got on this, because, again, the fate of this column, aside the surrender aspect of the biggest part of it, was not the topic of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the that mean that you did not ask for photographs of Muslim forces breaking through the area of defence where the losses were incurred and casualties?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not an intelligence officer at the OTP. I was an investigator, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us who made the selection of photographs that you were to study?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The selection was made by our request, and then we received material that matched or not our request. Who the -- at the final thing made the selection, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me why there is not a single aerial photograph showing the formation of the column, the movement of the column, when they encountered ambushes, breaking through, and so on? Thank you. The column of the 28th Division of the BH Army, I mean.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know, and I repeat it for many times again. I never made such a request, for the simple reason that the military history of this fall of the enclave is none of our business. Our business is to deal with the fate of a people who surrendered, who were captured, and who were under the control of the security branch of the Bosnian Serb Army. This is the guts of this case. The fate of this column, the battle, all this will -- may be in the history books of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we were to have a photograph of the fighting that was going on and the ambushes that they passed through, you would have the location as well at which the fatalities happened and where they were perhaps buried. Would you agree with that? Would you have that?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You had the same question yesterday. I told you that looking for the bodies of missing in action is the business of governments. It's not the business of the OTP to find the graves of people who have been killed in battle. Our goal is to find the graves of people who have been murdered.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ruez, can you tell me whether it was your task, as an OTP investigator, to provide something that would be of use to the Defence as well?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, and not only for the Defence, but for any other case that the OTP was dealing with, wherever the victims were Bosniaks or Serbs. And, indeed, this happened from time to time. It's a normal way of functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'll stop you. We didn't receive the interpretation. There was a problem, obviously. Could you please repeat the last question. There was no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I was asking Mr. Ruez, in view of his contacts with the representatives of the American government, whether he could, for the purposes of the Defence and the use of the Defence, access certain photographs that we need and not only photographs that the Prosecution needs for the indictment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I answered. I was working for the OTP, not trying to compile whatever evidence that would have confirmed the unconfirmable. What could, anyhow, not be confirmed was that nothing happened in Srebrenica. My answer is about the fact that if, indeed, we had came across information --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. Yes, I'm clear on that, and I'll have to move on to another area because my time is limited. And my first question is this: How often did you interview witnesses together with Mr. Peter McCloskey? Thank you. And may we have up on e-court 1D109 next, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I conducted a few interviews together with Peter McCloskey at the moment we were at the stage of interviewing personnel from the Bosnian Serb Army, so that was mainly, if I recall well, end of 1998, year 1999, and also part of 2000. The precise number of personnel we interviewed during that process, I could not remember well, but I would assess maybe -- maybe between 10 and 15 persons, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. We have the document on our screens, 1D109. May we have page 2 displayed, please. It's an interview -- the transcript of an interview with a Prosecution witness, Drazen Erdemovic, who appeared before this Tribunal, and it was conducted by Mr. Ruez and Mr. McCloskey. I'm going to read out a part of the instructions given to a witness, and after that I'm going to put a series of questions to you. Peter McCloskey says: "Another thing that's important for the Court, and not this coming-up court, but if there is a trial and you will be a witness for the Prosecution, it will be required by the Rules of Court that you answer the questions simply and directly, and it is actually much better for the lawyers that you answer that way in court because then we control -- we control how much information the Court sees." Now, my question -- first question to you is this: When the proofing session was held, was one of your aims to control the quantity of information that the Court is supposed to see? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me answer for my part. As an investigator, my goal, like an intelligence officer in the army, is to get as much information as possible. On the other hand, the professional activity of a prosecutor is not something that I'm supposed to discuss. I'm not a prosecutor. I was heading an investigation. Then the strategy of a prosecutor, it is really a question to be asked to the Prosecutor, not to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. Tell me what role you were in then, when you said that, and what role was Peter McCloskey in?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean during this specific interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That's right, yes, with Erdemovic.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's simple. All interviews with Drazen Erdemovic, my interest, in terms of an investigator, was to find as much to take out of him as much information he was ready to provide, and the role of the Prosecutor is also to inform him about his rights, the limits he should not overpass, the risk he takes when he says things that can involve himself, and so on. So there is a -- it's a kind of -- it's a role of legal advice to a person who is under interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And what function was he performing at the time? Mr. McCloskey, I mean. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not 100 per cent sure, but I would think that he was the trial attorney for the Erdemovic case at that time. I don't know the date of this interview, because we conducted many with Drazen Erdemovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But you didn't answer my previous question. Was it the purpose to control the information that the Court sees, yes or no? Because you gave us an extensive answer to the first question.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can only speak for myself, what my goal is. Reorient your question to the relevant person. I cannot answer in the name of another person.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. Now, on page 3 of that same transcript where you're proofing Mr. Erdemovic for his testimony, Mr. McCloskey says as follows, and I quote: "We're going to practice on concise -- precise answers to Mr. Ruez's questions. But we can make pauses when it comes to questions which are precise, and then you can explain to us whatever you want and you can talk about everything you wish to talk about." Do you remember how you practiced this, and am I right in saying that this was a proofing session -- or, rather, taking interviews from him, and while there were breaks you weren't recording that and he could say whatever he liked, but once you started recording, he couldn't say anything? Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this sounds very strange to me, this things about recording -- stopping recording. Either we record and we record absolutely everything from the first minute to the last one, and I actually even say from the first to the last second, or we don't record anything because we are in -- off conversation. So, no, I don't see the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you should be aware of the fact that you are -- your quotations are parts of those remarks of Mr. McCloskey, not of this witness. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. But here, the witness was present as an investigator, and he practiced with the witness, he drilled the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's not necessary to explain it. But if you put parts of this interview to this witness, you should be aware of the fact that you are only quoting those parts referring to Mr. McCloskey. And once -- some minutes ago, you just said, in your question, What you said there in this part of this interview, but it was, in fact, a part and there was a quotation of Mr. McCloskey. Be very careful, please. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It says: "We will practice on concise answers to Mr. Ruez's questions, but we can take breaks, and the precise questions you can talk to us about, what you feel you need to and anything you want." And that is what Peter McCloskey says to the witness, Mr. Erdemovic, and he is questioned by Mr. Ruez, so that's why I asked him. It's very important, what a proofing session looks like for a witness that is to appear in court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Proofing -- I think the date of this interview should be set out. It is nowhere near any trial.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There's no proofing session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I think the general knows what a proofing session is, and so I think this should be -- should be set out and at least the witness be given the date of this thing so we can put it in context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. President. This interview was conducted with Mr. Erdemovic on the 6th of November, 1996, and I asked this question because that same witness will be a witness in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's absolutely not necessary to explain why you ask a question. Please put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, but the Prosecutor wanted me to tell the witness when the interview was conducted, so I did. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I want to point out that as far as I see the thing, this is not a proofing session. I -- in my recollection, I never participated in any proofing session. The proofing session is between the witness and the Prosecutor. This was an interview, no proofing. We should see the start of it in order to make sure. Maybe the Prosecutor added, during this interview, some methodology for the witness in order to concede his answer and, in a way, in bracket, train him to answer properly the questions, but this is not a proofing session. This is an interview. I do not participate in proofing sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. Well, from the next question, we can see whether it was a preparatory meeting with you, proofing meeting, or for the Court. And I quote further, Mr. McCloskey, during the interview you had with Mr. Erdemovic, say --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we have a reference, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Page 7 of the transcript: "You were very good in taking on responsibility. The only reason for which I now mention this is that if you have any reason not to feel bad every time something bad happens, after some time the Judges will think --" so the Judges, not the investigators, "the Judges will think that you're not undertaking responsibility. So you need to tell the truth, as you have been doing, and explaining things. And we will do our best to help you convince the Judges about all the good things you have done so they understand that. Do you understand?" And then: "I'm just offering one piece of advice. I'm only offering you some advice, that if you always offer excuses all the time, it will start to turn around and look bad for you with the Judges. It is a combination of explaining them about things so they understand." Now, from this I take it that it was a proofing session, preparing him for appearing in court. Thank you. Now, my question is this: Can you explain to us all the things that you and Mr. McCloskey did to convince the Trial Chamber of the truth of Erdemovic's testimony?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only answer for myself. What I did was to take as many details as possible from Erdemovic's testimony in order to confront what he was saying with observations on the ground, scientific police analysis of the terrain, finding the mass grave he was talking about, and then finding the secondary graves in which this 1.200 people he alleged were killed that day had been buried, plus the 500 at Pilica Dom, a crime scene that without his assistance we would never have found because there was absolutely no survivor from this place. So what we did, indeed, to confirm the story of Erdemovic, at least the part of the story that we could confirm because linked with the crime scenes we were busy with, is what I just explained. That's what we did for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. At the time, did Mr. McCloskey tell Erdemovic the following: "Nothing will be used against you, the fact will not be used against you, whether you were there to arrest him, or kidnap him, or kill him, whether you're telling the truth or not"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May we have a reference, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to have a reference. Where do we find that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That quotation is taken from page 11. Thank you for your assistance, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only thing is that I have no clue of who we are referring to when it is said "arrest him," "kidnap him," or whatever. I don't know who --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Just a moment and I'll ask you the question. Thank you, Mr. Ruez. I'm going to ask you a question. And when you read the transcript on page 11, it is Mr. McCloskey talking to Mr. Erdemovic, who took part in the proofing session. Now, could you answer the next question, please. Did you prepare any witness, telling them how they should answer questions, questions that you assumed the opposite side, that is to say, the Defence, could ask them or the Trial Chamber? Just a yes-or-no answer, please. Did you prepare them or not?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not my role to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. Now, on page 16 of that same document - and may we have page 16 displayed on our screens, please, once again referring to Drazen Erdemovic - this is what was stated: "This is how it was, this is what happened: I told you we were ordered not to shoot at the civilians, because we called the civilians to come out, and I told you we were ordered not to shoot at the civilians." Now, my question to you is this: As an investigator, yourself, do you remember these facts, since they are very important for the investigation being conducted during a trial? Because it says that there was an order not to shoot at the civilians. So who issued that order, to the best of your knowledge, to Erdemovic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drazen Erdemovic, as you said, will come and testify. The recollection I have of this is that just before the 10th Sabotage Detachment Group entered -- I mean, went down the hill to enter Srebrenica, they had a short briefing where, indeed, some pieces of International Law were reminded to them, and I would think -- I don't remember, but the direct commander at that moment was Lieutenant Pellnas, so I believe this was a little chat from Lieutenant Pellnas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. Could the investigator be shown 65 ter 4037. While we wait for it to come up on the screens, I will tell you what kind of document this is. This is a document from the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska Army, dated the 9th of September, 1991, the author of which is the accused before you, and this in his role as the assistant commander for intelligence and security. In the relevant portions, it says -- can we have it before us? Do we see it? And I quote -- there is only one page to this document in Serbian: "The president of the republic is satisfied with the results of combat operations around Srebrenica and has agreed with the continuation of operations for the take-over of Srebrenica, disarming of Muslim terrorist gangs, and complete demilitarisation of the Srebrenica enclave. "The president of the republic ordered that in the follow-up combat operations, full protection be ensured to UNPROFOR members and the Muslim civilian population, and that they be guaranteed safety in the event of their cross-over to the territory of Republika Srpska." Now, this is the quoted portion, and then it reads on: "In accordance with the order of the president of Republika Srpska, you must issue an order to all combat units participating in combat operations around Srebrenica to offer maximum protection and safety to all UNPROFOR members and civilians, the civilian Muslim population -- and the civilian Muslim population. You must order subordinate units to refrain from destroying civilian targets unless forced to do so because of strong enemy resistance. Ban the torching of residential buildings, and treat the civilian population and war prisoners in accordance with the Geneva Conventions of 12 August 1949." I have now read out a portion of an order sent from the Main Staff on the 9th of July, 1995. Now, my question for you is this: Have you had occasion to see this document before, the document that I was quoting from, while you were an investigator for the OTP? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This one, no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to tender this document into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I see a problem. The witness said that he doesn't know anything about this document. He hasn't seen it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That's exactly what I asked him, whether he had seen it while he was an investigator, and he said he didn't. And this shows that Erdemovic, too, could have been issued this order, because I asked him prior to this whether they had been given orders not to open fire on civilians, and now I quoted from this order that was also issued to Erdemovic. And I would like to tender it into evidence because Erdemovic will come to testify in this trial. And we can ask the witness whether this is the same order that was mentioned during the proofing sessions conducted with Mr. Erdemovic by Mr. Ruez and McCloskey. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution has no objection to this going into evidence. It will be discussed by many witnesses and is a fundamental document for the Prosecution as well as, apparently, the Defence, so I see no harm in it going in. It might be good that you just have full access to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise to interpreters for the noises that I'm causing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view that this may be a very important document. However, it will not be received with the evidence of this witness. It may be tendered by either party at a later stage with another witness, just to follow the normal procedure in this trial. You should think about some other documents you have used with this witness if you want to tender them. But now carry on, please, Mr. Tolimir. This one will not be received at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, do you remember whether Mr. Erdemovic told you that they had been ordered not to shoot at civilians? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember precisely what this -- his statement was about this little moment before they entered the town and found this man who they beat up and slit his throat. I don't remember the content. There is most certainly a paragraph in his interview that details this, this aspect, but I don't remember this part of the interview. That was an interview and not a proofing session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. Did I quote the conversation or the interview that you conducted together with Mr. McCloskey with Mr. Erdemovic and that we see before us here on page 16?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't have that on the screen anymore.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we then please pull that document back up on the screen, because it's very important. Erdemovic said: "I told you that we were ordered not to shoot at civilians." Thank you. Now, if this is irrelevant for the Court, it's fine, I can just move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The question was if you -- if the accused quoted correctly from this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, and I think the people on the spot obeyed. They did not shoot; they just slit their throat.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. In view of the fact that a criminal -- that a crime was committed, it is important to know that he said that there had been an order about not shooting at civilians, and this document was offered as proof of that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, my next question is -- I can no longer dwell on this because of time constraints, so I will quote again your words from the interview to "The Monitor." That's 1D60, on page 7. Could we please pull up document 1D60, and that will be page 8 in the English translation. We have been provided a translation, I've just been informed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we please see always the first page first so that we know what it is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. While we are looking at this first page, I will say, Mr. Ruez, to you that in response to the reporter from "Monitor," you say: "General Milan Gvero and Zdravko Tolimir from the Main Staff have been mentioned on several occasions in the Krstic trial." And your reply was, and I quote --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we now have page 7 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Page 8 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English, that's on page 8. Can we go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Ruez answers: "Yes, they were mentioned. At this point, I would leave Gvero aside. This does not mean there is nothing there. Tolimir is an entirely different kind of story, and that is why these investigations need to be long-term." Can we have the next page of this document: "That is why these investigations need to be long-term. We were never able to talk to Tolimir. People did not say much about him. The main organiser in Srebrenica from the Intelligence and Security Service were under his command. The chief organisers from Srebrenica, from the Security Services, were under his command. "Monitor: Do you mean -- do you think he is in Belgrade, Ruez? "I don't know where he is. Probably only a small circle knows where he is, and where he was, and what he did in Srebrenica. Maybe he was fishing on the Drina. But during the Zepa operation, he was in the field, and as a security person, he tried to separated people. I don't know what he did in Srebrenica. It would be interesting to investigate deeper into Tolimir's role, if at all, because he was one of those who has been somewhat neglected in the entire case." My question, Mr. Ruez, is this: Is this what you stated, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In this trial, at the very beginning, you said that you did not investigate the events in Zepa, and here you are discussing what General Tolimir did in Zepa. If you did not investigate the Zepa incident, how, then, can you claim that what he did there was separate people? And the second question that I have for you is: Have you ever heard anyone say that Tolimir was in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the first question, yes, indeed, I confirm I did not take part in the investigation regarding the events in Zepa. But, on the other hand, working at the OTP and knowing the connection between, at least in the close chronology, Zepa and Srebrenica, I had also access to information that I will say off records, and this is the reason why I dropped this info to this journalist, though, indeed, I was not officially in charge of that part of investigation. But I don't doubt that since it's part of your indictment, this evidence will be brought in front of the Court. And for the second part of your question, yeah, regarding your presence in Srebrenica, indeed, except if things changed after my departure in 2001, we have no photograph or record of your presence in Srebrenica town during the dates of the 11, 12, and 13, but maybe the Prosecution has something on this. I personally have no recollection of your physical presence on the -- on these spots.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say that Tolimir was neglected in the investigation, what do you mean exactly? Do you mean that there were no statements -- witness statements about Tolimir, or are you referring to something else, that simply no investigations were conducted into Tolimir's case?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The journalist probably didn't quote me well, because I never say "Tolimir," I always say "General Tolimir," but that's a detail. It's not a reality that you were neglected. It's because, indeed, such an investigation takes a lot of time. The reason why it needs continuity and, in this instance, to determine the responsibility of the ones and the others, it needs to go from the bottom to the top and not from the top to the bottom, so I think that the rest of the presentation the Prosecutor builds his case around will be, no doubt -- I don't doubt to show that, indeed, the persons who have been in charge of all the logistical aspect, let's say, in terms of finding locations and preparing things, were, indeed, members of the security branch of the Bosnian Serb Army. So this is maybe the reason why I said that General Tolimir had been neglected. But I see it has not been neglected too long, because after my departure there was an indictment against you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. We will now move on to my next question. You said the following about General Mladic in "The Monitor" interview, and that will be on page 9 of the English version: "I don't know him, but I think that he is the kind of man who is capable of taking a challenge on the spot -- accepting a challenge on the spot. For instance, at sick man would come up with a sudden idea, Let's kill them all." Mladic would hook up or tag on to that in view of the things that he publicly said in 1994 and the intention to annihilate Muslims for Muslim reasons, and all these things are, in fact --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not find the part that is being quoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So did you say this or didn't you say this? I'm just asking you to confirm so I can move on.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, I could not. But what I could confirm is that he reiterated his will as soon as 11 July, since we have him on film saying that this was -- the time had come to take revenge on the Turks. So it was an additional quote that I could add to this, but that's part of General Mladic's case. And I would add, also, the same idea, that these promises are made sometimes written and sometimes orally, that we also have him on film reassuring the population that no one would harm them and they had nothing to fear, so that's a bit of follow-up of the written order. He gave it even orally, with additional promises.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now please be shown 1D59. This is the statement that Mr. Ruez made before the -- in the French parliamentary hearings, and he said the following --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The greatest surprise was the attitude of General Mladic --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you tendering this "Monitor" article?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I asked yesterday for it to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I just got the information we have that already as an exhibit, D30 [sic]. Thank you. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I now quote Mr. Ruez's words, his statement before the Parliamentary Committee, page 7 of the Serbian: "The greatest surprise was the attitude of General Mladic in 1994, when he gave an interview to a newspaper whose title I cannot recall." This is what you said. You can see it before you. What uprising from the early 19th century are you referring to here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we get a specific reference to the English so that Mr. Ruez can read this, so that we can all follow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It would be very helpful. And I take the opportunity to correct myself. On page 31, line 11, it should be "D31." Can you give a reference, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's on page 7 in the English version, the last paragraph on the page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, do you find the question of the accused --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but never mind, I understand the question. I mean, I'm not a historian, but it's always the same historical reference to the battle where the Serbs tried to stop the Ottomans.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. But I asked you whether you could tell us what statement of General Mladic's was this where he actually spoke about his objectives relating and in reference to Srebrenica? I could not find any such statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember either, but I would think it could be found in the documentation that is prepared by the OTP in case of a future trial of General Mladic. But I don't have the record in memory either. But, again, though I don't remember this one, we have on videotape his comments dated 11 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You were referring to 1994 here, so this was before Srebrenica and not what General Mladic said after Srebrenica. This here is a reference to 1994. It says: "The most surprising aspect in this was the attitude of General Mladic ... in 1994." So did you read then something about this even before Srebrenica? It's very important for this Trial Chamber to know about, if you had any such knowledge. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also realise it will be very important to find this record for the day of the trial of General Mladic, if ever. For the purpose of this one, I'm sorry to say that I don't remember the reference of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. May God bless Mladic, but we will not talk about this. I only asked you, since you gave this statement before the Parliament, to repeat it here before this Trial Chamber. Now, let us go back to the objectives of your investigation and what type of instructions you gave to those who worked on trying to find mass graves. Were numerous experts engaged for that purpose, including forensics experts? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could the witness please be shown the report prepared by Mr. Haglund. That's 1D56. Thank you. While we wait for the document to come up on the screens, let me tell the witness that this is an expert report provided by Professor Garland [as interpreted], whom you know. He's a crime officer, and he was working on a forensic investigation of the Cerska locality mass grave. After we've seen the first page, could we please see page 10 in the Serbian version, second paragraph. And in English, that will be on page 9, the third paragraph. Thank you. Thank you. We have the Serbian version, and in a moment you will also see it in English on the left-hand side of the screen. Could we see page 9, please, paragraph 3. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Page 9, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The autopsy of the witness -- of the victims began on the 31st of July, 1996, and lasted until 22nd August 1996.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could we have page 9 of the English version, please, in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I've been informed now that the correct page is on the monitor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "Autopsy examinations were carried out at a temporary morgue established at a war-damaged clothing factory on the outskirts of the town of Kalesija in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Autopsy examinations were carried out under the direction of Dr. Robert H. Kirchner, director of the International Forensic Programme of Physicians for Human Rights." "Finalisation of cause and manner of death, as well as editing of final autopsy reports, was facilitated by ICTY legal adviser," the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, in other words, "Peter McCloskey." My question is this: Mr. Ruez, the examination and establishing the causes and manner of death, did that mean that what you were supposed to establish was whether someone was killed execution-style, or killed in combat, or in some other way? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As an investigator, it is, indeed, my role to find -- ask people to find out about these questions, but it's not my role to do it personally. This is why there are experts doing this type of assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. What I asked you was this: The establishment of the cause and manner of death, does that mean that what needs to be established first was whether somebody was killed in action, not who did it, but whether he was killed in action, whether they were executed, killed by shelling, and so on?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I repeat, this is absolutely the role of someone who is leading such an investigation, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. Answer this next question, please. What place and role did Mr. Peter McCloskey play in the team?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, the structure of the team was that there was an investigation team leader. That was myself. And there was a legal adviser, who was Mr. Peter McCloskey. So the role of Peter McCloskey as the legal adviser in such a team is to make sure that the material we collect would be ready for presentation to a courtroom, and so assess the quality of the material in order to make sure if we can use it or if we cannot use it in a courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think, taking into account the time, we must have our first break now. And we adjourn and resume quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir and Mr. Gajic, I would like to raise some question. We are quite concerned about the time when we received the new notification about exhibits -- about documents you want to use during the cross-examination of this witness. Yesterday, in the afternoon during our hearing, you notified the Chamber, the Registry, and the Prosecution about the list of witnesses, and you did that today again. I would like to remind you that we have issued an order with the guidance of, I think, 22nd of February, that this notification should be sent to the other party and to the Registry 24 or 48 hours in advance. This is a very late stage during cross-examination, and this is not the appropriate and proper way to deal with that problem. Not to waste time, we should continue cross-examination, but please bear in mind, Mr. Tolimir, that you should finish with your cross-examination half past 6.00 of today's hearing so that the Prosecution has the possibility for re-examination. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to say good afternoon to everybody in this courtroom and all those attending the trial, and may God's will be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, I have another question. Mr. Ruez, a moment ago we spoke about Haglund's report, and just to remind you, he says: "Informing the ultimate conclusions and the drafting of a final version of the autopsy reports, I was assisted by the legal adviser of the ICTY, Peter McCloskey." Now, my question to you is this: Is it the role of a legal adviser to establish the cause of death and manner of death and to draft possible reports, or is that the work of a forensic expert? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There's no indication in the record that the Prosecutor was taking part in establishing cause of death. To assume a fact that's not in evidence of that nature is improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. And I think, if I recall that correctly, the witness answered that question about his role into investigations of cause of death.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I quoted from the document a moment ago. 1D56 was the number of the document, so may we have it called up again, please. It was a report by Professor Haglund, the crime and forensic investigation of the Cerska mass grave, and I quoted his last sentence where he said that in the drafting of the final autopsy report, they were assisted by the legal adviser of the ICTY, Peter McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Would you please indicate and give a reference where you and we can find this portion?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D56, page 10. It's the last sentence on that page. Thank you. It's the last sentence of the third paragraph in English: "Finalisation of cause and manner of death," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In fact, I don't find it, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have that portion highlighted for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, I found it. And please now put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was asking the witness, and let me repeat the question, this:

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is it the role of a legal adviser to establish the cause and manner of death, and in editing a final autopsy report, or is that the work of a forensic expert? Thank you, Witness. And could you please answer the question, Mr. Ruez?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I think this witness will be able to answer this question in a proper way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President. However, he's deliberately misstating this paragraph. It says "facilitated," and he is misstating it. And I don't think it's fair to require the witness to read every deliberate misstatement into a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It was quoted, and it is on the record, that the word, in fact, is "facilitated." And the witness will be able to answer this question. Mr. Ruez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My answer is that I was not an eye-witness of the situation when the legal adviser, at that time Mr. Peter McCloskey, provided, indeed, the guide-lines to the experts in order that they do not commit mistakes in the way they would present their documentation. But what I know as a fact is that never, ever the legal adviser would have interfered with the experts in order to assist them determining the cause of death. This in no way happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. Now, is what I quoted from the report correct, the report from Professor Haglund? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I share the opinion of the Prosecutor when he says you are misreading and misinterpreting what is written in Bill Haglund's reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. Now, whether I interpreted it or -- did I interpret it or did I quote Dr. Haglund's report? I didn't interpret anything. I was just quoting from the report. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What is your question, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is as follows: At that time when this report was tabled by the professor, was Mr. Ruez subordinate -- or, rather, superior to Mr. McCloskey, was he superior -- in a superior position to Mr. McCloskey? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Superior position" is not the way to put it. I was the investigation team leader. Peter McCloskey was the legal adviser. We took, more or less, all our decisions in common. We had no feeling one was the superior of the other. We were rowing in the same boat.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Ruez. Now, may we have the first page displayed and the 10th page in Serbian displayed, and it's -- or, rather, I'd like to tender page 1 and 10 of the Serbian version and page 9 of the English into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, may we offer the entire document into evidence so that you may make sense of this? I believe it's been offered under the expert Rule 94 bis, perhaps, and I believe Haglund is 92 bis. But, in any event, these -- Haglund and his reports have been offered to this Chamber under the Rules of Procedures and Evidence, and it's -- we have no objection to it coming in, but it should be coming in in a whole so that you can see it all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, Mr. President. Professor Haglund is due to appear as a Prosecution witness here, and he's going to testify about the report that he drafted and tabled, and then Mr. McCloskey can tender the document into evidence. And it's practice here that we tender and admit into evidence those portions which are of interest for a particular witness and linked to a particular witness, which the witness can confirm. So I would now like to tender just what I said, page 1 and 10 of the Serbian version and page 9 of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber will receive the two pages offered by the accused, and the other portions may be received as an exhibit at a later stage of this case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D35, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I've just been informed that we have offered Dr. Haglund's report 92 bis, and so it could be that he does not come here, though we will perhaps reconsider whether we offer him as 92 ter. But I just wanted to make sure that that's clear from the record. He may not come here, pending the outcome of the motion, but we'll, of course, consider it and as the issues have been presented themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that information. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ruez, let's move on to another area, since we have used up quite a lot of time on this topic. On page 7 of the transcript, lines 20 to 22, you drew conclusions in the investigation as to the reasons why people were leaving Srebrenica, and I quote - these are your words: "As you probably know, the conclusion of the investigation was that in Potocari the conduct of the Bosnian Army was geared towards instilling fear in people so that they should leave the area of their own free will." Are those your words? And you can look back to the transcript. It's page 7, lines 20 to 22. May we have that displayed, please, if necessary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I confirm these are my words.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now may we have the video-recording of the first meeting from the Fontana Hotel, 1995. It lasts for about two and a half minutes of a total of nine minutes, so from nine minutes thirty-six --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Tolimir repeat the times, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, could you please repeat the times, as requested by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D111 is the number of the document, from nine minutes thirty-four seconds to twelve minutes fifteen seconds. It's a portion of a conversation when General Mladic is asking questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "I had a talk with --"

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, since we've just seen this excerpt, this footage, which has taken up quite a bit of my time, could I ask you to give brief answers. Now, we heard during that excerpt -- or, rather, have you ever seen this footage before? Thank you. Yes or no, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen it many times before, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you see Karremans -- or, rather, General Mladic asking why he was looking for him?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic at that time was desperately looking for a representative of Bosniak Muslim community there, mainly for representatives of the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell me what you heard on this footage? Who was looking for whom? Was it Mladic looking for Karremans or Karremans asking for a meeting with Mladic? Which was it?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know this is only a very short extract of a long footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I know that, but I don't have the time to show the entire footage. But did you hear General Mladic say, Why were you looking for me?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because Colonel Karremans wants to discuss the issue of the population which remains within the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So was it -- did Colonel Karremans explain to Mladic why he was looking for him; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we can see it on the film, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My second question: When this meeting was held at the Fontana, was the Serb Army in Potocari? Thank you. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not the 12, in the evening, not the 11, in the evening. They arrived at 12, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My third question: Where were the military-able men at that time that had come to the base; members of the BH Army, that is?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you know, most of the members of the BiH Army took off that evening of the 11 to the north of the enclave, to exfiltrate out of the enclave. Those who arrived in Potocari the 11 were, indeed, among them able men, may be [Realtime transcript read in error "mainly"] also members of the 28 Division, but mainly family members, women, elderly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Colonel Karremans, did he make a list of the able-bodied men? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to point out a mistake in the transcript. It's not "mainly members of the 28th Division," but "may be some members." It's not the same thing. Line 19 -- 16. Returning to the list, yes, I know a list of people who were inside the compound of the UN. The beginning of the list was drafted at that time, indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The able-bodied, is that what you mean; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about a list of those who managed to take refuge within the UN compound. As you know, most of the people were outside, but the UN battalion, despite of the threats of General Mladic, accepted to receive approximately 5.000 people within the UN compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. We'll come back to the list later on and the number, the figure. The list exists with the United Nations. And now I'd like to move on to another area, but we'll come back to the Fontana Hotel meeting as well. However, for the moment, could you look at some more footage, and I'd like to hear your comments to what we're going to show you. Thank you. Mr. Ruez, do you know there's a film called "Resolution 819," where the main character is, in fact, you? Have you ever seen that film, that footage?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us just briefly take a look at a few of the frames of this video-clip just to get an idea what it's about. Could we please see 1D76, page 1, and then after that page 2. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see page 2. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, could you please tell us whether you are the Jean-Rene Ruez mentioned here? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now see page 3, please, where we will see that the text speaks for itself. Thank you. Is this enough for your information, so we can move on to page 4? Can we now see page 4, please. Thank you. We have page 4 before us, and we can read on the screen: "The former Yugoslavia in 1995. The war is reaching its apex. The Muslim enclave of Srebrenica is at the point of falling into the hands of the Bosnian Serbs under the command of General Mladic and under orders from Radovan Karadzic. The civilian population is under the protection of the UN Resolution 819." Can we see the next page, please: "The film is inspired by true events, but some characters are completely fictitious."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question, Mr. Ruez, is this: The character playing you in this movie, his name is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You want me to tell you the name of the actor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: No. Could you just tell the Trial Chamber whether the personal -- the character called Calvez in the film, whether that is actually you?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not the one who drafted the scenario. I never met, except once when the film went out, the actor supposed to play my character. Since, indeed, the person who wrote that scenario inspired himself from part of my activities, and it was written on one of the exhibits, I have, indeed, the feeling that Calvez is supposed to be Ruez. But more than that, I don't know, because I didn't take any part into the conception and the realisation of that fiction based on some reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. Could we now please see on the monitors page 7. That is a photograph, a still from this video-clip, 38 minutes 24 seconds. Mr. Ruez, could you tell us, who is depicted in this photo?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have nothing on my screen. Have I something?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I thought you had it, because I have it before me.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is General Tolimir, as far as I recognise, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. Could we now see page 8, please. That's the photograph 38 minutes 38 seconds. Thank you. Mr. Ruez, could you tell us who is depicted in this photo? Can you identify the persons?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Who is this individual in the Republika Srpska Army uniform, with a cap on his head? Thank you. Could you tell us who that person is, if you know?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He looks a bit like Mr. Vasic, but since he has a military hat, it's not him. Is that you?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Who is standing next to Mr. Tolimir in the photograph? If you identified me there, who is next to this uniformed person, and is this the individual or the actor playing your character, called Calvez, in the movie?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, according to his glasses he's wearing and his profile, it could be Benoit Magimel.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see the next photo, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, do you have a question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have several questions. I would just like to show the photos that we have selected, and then I would invite Mr. Ruez to comment on them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, could you tell us, who is depicted in this photograph, the man with the glasses?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, I have to insist on one thing. I can comment Mickey Mouse also for you in this courtroom, but I have absolutely nothing to do in the conception and the realisation of this film.
